1.title: Is it the preference training, or just seeing good examples?
1.description: We trained the legal specialist with SFT on only the preferred answers from its ORPO training pairs. It became the most cautious version, but it hedged even where nothing called for it, and its caution held up worst in the final answer.
1.size: 1 run per scenario, 7 scenarios per version
1.why: In earlier work, with one run per scenario, ORPO preference training on the legal specialist, Saul, had given only a small rise in caution. But that caution appeared only where the question called for it, and it held up in the editor's final answer better than any other version. Prompting had given a bigger rise, but earlier tests found it appearing where no caveats were needed and being stripped by the editor. We wrote down in advance that this cell alone could overturn that result. ORPO teaches a model to prefer one answer of a pair over the other. Was it that preference that mattered, or simply seeing the good answers? So we trained Saul with SFT (supervised fine-tuning, which trains directly on example answers) on only the preferred answers from the same pairs. The LoRA fine-tuning settings, number of steps and random seed were the same. Only the training objective differed.

expectations.text: SFT on the preferred answers alone would give weaker or less well-targeted caution than ORPO. That would show that learning which answer is better matters, not only seeing good examples.
expectations.note: SFT gave more caution than ORPO but used it on the control question too, 1.59 against 0.00, and its caution held up worst in the final answer.

1.found:
SFT gave the legal specialist the biggest rise in caution: 1.69 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters, against 0.82 for the untouched copy and 1.00 for ORPO. But it used that caution everywhere. On the control question, which calls for no caveats, the SFT version scored 1.59 and the ORPO version 0.00.

The SFT version's caution also held up worst in the editor's final answer. On a combined caution score for the final answer, SFT scored 0.443, below even the untouched copy at 0.624. ORPO scored highest, at 0.738.

This matched what prompting had done in earlier work: caution that appears whether or not it is called for, and that the editor strips out. Each version had one run on each of the 7 scenarios.
1.means: At the time, we concluded that learning which of two answers is better, the one thing SFT lacks, was what made ORPO's caution both well targeted and lasting. We updated our one-sentence summary. Training on examples and prompting change what a model says. Preference training changes when it says it, and only preference-trained caution survives the editor. Cell 2 then repeated every version five times per scenario.
1.later: Cell 2 repeated the comparison with five runs per scenario. SFT's excess caution on the control question held up. But ORPO's higher caution at the specialist and its top final score turned out to be noise, and the summary was revised. From 9 August the project no longer accepted the keyword counter behind these scores as a measuring tool, so they are treated as provisional.

51.label: Result
51.title: SFT on good answers alone gives loud but untargeted caution
51.summary: SFT raised the legal specialist's caution the most, 1.69 against 0.82 untouched and 1.00 for ORPO, but scored 1.59 on the control question where ORPO scored 0.00. It also had the lowest caution score in the final answer. We recorded the expectation as holding up strongly.

2.title: Do the early results hold up with five runs per scenario?
2.description: We ran four versions of the legal specialist five times on each of 7 scenarios. The editor's stripping of extra caution held up, and so did ORPO's drop on the control question. ORPO's apparent rise in caution turned out to be noise.
2.why: Cell 1 and the earlier work rested on one run per scenario, so any difference could have been chance. The plan called for five runs of every version on all 7 scenarios, with a plausible range around each result. We compared four versions of the legal specialist. They were the untouched copy, a version prompted with a description of the caution we wanted, and the ORPO and SFT versions from Cell 1. We did not write down specific expectations for this cell. Its job was to show which earlier differences were real.
2.found:
Two findings held up. First, prompting and SFT both raised caution at the specialist well above the untouched copy: 1.85 and 1.77 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters, against 0.89. But on the combined caution score for the final answer, both came out at or below the untouched copy, at 0.590 and 0.575 against 0.859. The editor stripped their extra caution.

Second, ORPO was the only version that became less cautious on the control question: 0.15, against 0.96 for the untouched copy. The prompted version scored 3.03 there and SFT 1.21.

One finding did not hold up. ORPO's small rise at the specialist and its top final score in Cell 1 were noise. With five runs, ORPO showed no clear difference from the untouched copy on either, at 0.87 at the specialist and 0.655 in the final answer. An earlier fourfold rise on one scenario also disappeared.
2.means: With 91 training pairs, ORPO added little caution. What set it apart was that it harmed nothing and was the only method that reduced caution where none was needed. We revised the one-sentence summary. Prompting and training on examples add loud, untargeted caution that the editor strips. Preference training at this amount adds little, but it is the only method that improves when a model is cautious rather than how much. Whether more training pairs would help became the first open question, ahead of Cells 3 to 5.
2.later: The data audit of 1 August found that each set of five runs mixed one run from an earlier session with four from a later one. In three of the four versions, answers from the two sessions differed in length by a consistent 5 to 8%. No ranges changed, and the paper's limitations disclosed it. From 9 August the keyword counter was no longer accepted as a measuring tool, so these scores are treated as provisional.

99.label: Result
99.title: Five runs per scenario: which early differences were real
99.summary: Prompting and SFT raised the legal specialist's caution well above the untouched copy, but the editor stripped it. ORPO alone cut caution on the control question, to 0.15 against 0.96. ORPO's apparent rise in caution from Cell 1 turned out to be noise.

3.title: Does the legal training effect repeat on other specialists?
3.description: We trained the healthcare and finance specialists with ORPO, as we had the legal one. Neither became more cautious. Neither repeated the legal specialist's drop in caution on the control question, where the healthcare model was already at zero.
3.why: By now ORPO's one distinctive effect on the legal specialist, Saul, was less caution on a question that called for no caveats. One specialist is a thin basis for a claim, so the plan repeated the training on the other two. We built training pairs for each the same way and checked that none overlapped with the test scenarios. The finance model, Qwen-Open-Finance, had been through SFT only, so like Saul it was lightly aligned, and we expected it to repeat Saul's result. The healthcare model, Med42, had already been through preference training by its makers, so we expected a smaller effect there. Each ORPO version was compared with an untrained copy of the same model, with the legal specialist held at its untrained version.

expectations.text: ORPO on the finance specialist, Qwen-Open-Finance, would repeat the legal result: more caution, a pass on the control question, and caution that lasts into the final answer.
expectations.note: No rise in caution (1.37 untrained, 1.32 trained) and no drop on the control question, where the score went from 0.81 to 1.21. Later checks dropped the reading that ORPO made it worse.

expectations.text: ORPO on the healthcare specialist, Med42, which its makers had already preference-trained, would have a smaller effect than on the finance specialist.
expectations.note: No rise in caution (1.30 to 1.40) and nothing to fix on the control question. The finance model was not yet available, so the comparison was made against the legal specialist.

3.found:
Healthcare (Med42): caution at the specialist was 1.30 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters untrained and 1.40 after ORPO, no clear difference. On the control question, both versions scored 0.00 over 5 runs each, with the specialist consulted every time. There was nothing for ORPO to remove. The final answers showed no clear difference either, 0.723 and 0.690.

Finance (Qwen-Open-Finance): caution at the specialist was 1.37 untrained and 1.32 after ORPO, again no clear difference. On the control question the untrained model scored 0.81, so, as with Saul, there was room to improve. Instead the ORPO version scored 1.21. The final answers showed no clear difference, 0.637 and 0.704.

The control-question scores rest on only 5 runs per version. The finance model also has a built-in reasoning mode, a second difference that could affect its scores. Neither point rescues the expected result, since there was no sign of a drop.
3.means: ORPO did not raise caution on any of the three specialists, which come from three model families (Mistral, Llama-3 and Qwen3). Its one distinctive benefit, less caution where none is needed, appeared only on the legal specialist. Med42 gave it nothing to act on, and the finance model did not show it. The paper's claim that ORPO improves targeting had to be limited to the legal specialist.
3.later: Cells 7a and 7b re-checked the finance result. The NLI model found no increase on the control question, and the AI judges could not settle it. So the claim that ORPO made the finance model worse was dropped, and the result became no effect. The lack of a rise in caution held on the NLI model too. The keyword-counter scores are treated as provisional.

238.label: Result
238.title: Healthcare specialist: ORPO had nothing left to improve
238.summary: ORPO on Med42 gave no clear rise in caution, 1.40 against 1.30. The untrained model already scored 0.00 on the control question, so there was nothing to reduce. We recorded the smaller effect we expected, measured against the legal specialist because the finance model was not yet available.

267.label: Result
267.title: Finance specialist: the legal result did not repeat
267.summary: ORPO on Qwen-Open-Finance gave no rise in caution, 1.32 against 1.37. On the control question it scored 1.21 against 0.81 untrained, the wrong direction. ORPO's benefit on targeting had appeared only on the legal specialist, so the paper's claim was limited to that specialist.

4.title: Does the legal training work on other base models?
4.description: We planned to apply the legal training pairs to two other base models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and compare the effect with Saul's. This cell was never run.
4.why: Saul, our legal specialist, is built on Mistral-7B-v0.1. The original plan asked whether the same training pairs would work on two base models that their makers had already aligned more thoroughly. We expected the effect to appear on those models too, but to be smaller than on Saul. This would have shown whether the training effect depends on the starting model.

expectations.text: The same legal training pairs would also work on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, but with a smaller effect than on Saul.
expectations.note: Never tested, because the cell was never run.

4.found: This cell was never run. No models were trained or scored for it.
4.means: The plan's expectation P4 was never tested. The closest evidence came from Cell 3. It trained specialists from two other model families, Med42 (Llama-3) and Qwen-Open-Finance (Qwen3), on their own healthcare and finance pairs, not on the legal ones.

5.title: Does a second preference-training method, CPO, work the same way?
5.description: We trained the legal specialist with CPO instead of ORPO, keeping everything else the same. CPO also cut caution on the control question, to under half the untouched level, but it cut caution on the real questions too.
5.why: After Cell 7, the legal specialist's drop in caution on the control question was the paper's only positive training result, backed by three scoring methods. We wanted to know whether it belonged to ORPO alone or to this type of preference training in general. CPO is a second preference-training method that, like ORPO, trains without a separate reference model. We used the same base model, Saul, and the same original 91 training pairs, rebuilt from the saved logs and checked to match the sizes of the original split. The LoRA settings, 364 training steps and random seed were also the same. Only the training objective changed. Because of Cell 7, we scored the control question with both the keyword counter and the NLI model, and required both to agree.

expectations.text: CPO would not raise the amount of caution at the legal specialist, just as ORPO had not.
expectations.note: No rise. Caution on the real questions fell instead, from 0.89 to 0.56 per 1,000 characters, with ranges that still slightly overlapped.

expectations.text: CPO would cut caution on the control question below the untouched level on both scoring methods, to at most half of it on the keyword counter.
expectations.note: It fell to 0.37 against 0.96 on the keyword counter and to 0.45 against 1.06 on the NLI model, about 0.4 times the untouched level on both.

5.found:
CPO cut caution on the control question to 0.37 on the keyword counter, against 0.96 for the untouched copy. On the NLI model's check for out-of-date warnings it scored 0.45, against 1.06. That is about 0.4 times the untouched level on both, under the bar of one half we had set in advance. ORPO had reached 0.15 and 0.35.

CPO did not raise caution on the real questions. It lowered it, from 0.89 to 0.56 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters, with ranges that still slightly overlapped. ORPO had not done this (0.87). We then divided caution on the control question by caution on the real questions, a measure we had not planned. Lower means better targeted. The untouched copy scored 1.08, CPO 0.66 and ORPO 0.17. CPO dampened caution everywhere, while ORPO's drop was aimed at places where caution was not needed.
5.means: The drop in unneeded caution came from this type of preference training in general, not from a quirk of ORPO. But only ORPO's drop was well targeted. The evidence for the paper's second result now read as follows. Preference training did not raise caution, across three model families, two scoring methods and 3.2 times more data. The legal drop appeared under both ORPO and CPO, ORPO alone was well targeted, and the drop did not repeat on the healthcare or finance specialists.
5.later: Later checks weakened the scoring behind this result. Cell 23 found the NLI model could not detect which kinds of caveat a sentence contained, and too few out-of-date warnings existed even to check that kind. From 9 August the keyword counter was no longer accepted as a measuring tool, so these figures are treated as provisional.

460.label: Plan
460.title: Plan: repeat the legal training with CPO instead of ORPO
460.summary: Same base model, same original 91 training pairs, same settings and seed as the first ORPO version, with only the training objective changed, over 35 runs. We expected no rise in caution and a drop on the control question to at most half the untouched level, with both scoring methods agreeing.

490.label: Result
490.title: CPO also cuts unneeded caution, but less selectively
490.summary: CPO cut caution on the control question to about 0.4 times the untouched level on both scoring methods, so the drop is not unique to ORPO. It also lowered caution on the real questions, which ORPO had not done, so only ORPO's drop was well targeted.

6.title: Does the editor, not the specialists, set the final caution level?
6.description: We ran three editor models with and without the instruction to keep the specialists' caveats. Each editor had its own typical level, extra caution from the specialists did not pass through, and removing the instruction cut caution 2 to 5 times.
6.why: The original plan asked whether caveats would survive the editor with all three of our local editor models, Phi-4, gpt-oss-20B and Qwen2.5-7B. It also asked whether prompted caution would weaken without the instruction telling the editor to keep the specialists' caveats. By the time this cell ran, Cell 2 and Cell 10 had suggested a simpler idea. The editor seems to write at its own habitual level of caution, largely whatever the specialists hand over. Stripping would then be what happens when very cautious input meets an editor with a fixed level. If so, different editors should show different levels, and the instruction should shift the level if instructions matter at all.

expectations.text: Caveats would survive the editor with all three local editor models, and caution that came only from prompting would weaken when the instruction to keep caveats was removed.
expectations.note: The notebook gave no direct pass or fail. The same pattern appeared with all three editors, and removing the instruction cut caution for every editor and both kinds of input.

6.found:
Each editor had its own typical level, largely independent of what the specialists handed over. With the instruction and ordinary specialist input, Qwen2.5 wrote 1.24 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters, Phi-4 1.17 and gpt-oss-20B 0.63.

Extra caution from the specialists did not pass through, and sometimes the opposite happened. We swapped in the SFT-trained legal specialist from Cell 1, which made the input 2 to 3 times more cautious. Phi-4's final answers then fell from 1.17 to 0.61, and Qwen2.5's fell slightly. Very cautious input seemed to be treated as stylistic noise.

Removing the instruction made final answers 2 to 5 times less cautious for every editor. With ordinary input, gpt-oss-20B fell from 0.63 to 0.20 and Qwen2.5 from 1.24 to 0.24. The notebook recorded this as a prediction overturned: instructions matter.
6.means: We refined the explanation for the paper. Caution in the final answer depends mainly on the editor's habitual level and its instructions, and hardly at all on what the specialists supply. The last writer sets the tone. Caution added upstream cannot push through it, and too much of it can make the editor pull back. ORPO's caution had seemed to survive only because it never went above the editor's level, while prompting and SFT went above it and were stripped. This led to Cells 6b and 6c: training the editor directly, and testing the instruction in steps.
6.later: Cell 8b later found that without instructions, models produce almost no caveats. The differences between editors were then reread as differences in how strongly each responds to its instructions. PD-13 then found the instruction's effect was mostly the editor typing the exact phrases it names. An audit confirmed all 72 runs consulted all three specialists. The keyword-counter figures are treated as provisional.

179.label: Result
179.title: Each editor has its own level, and the instruction sets it
179.summary: Across three editor models, final caution stayed near each editor's own level whatever the specialists supplied, and very cautious input could even lower it. Removing the instruction to keep caveats made final answers 2 to 5 times less cautious for every editor, which the notebook recorded as a prediction overturned.

6b.title: Can training the editor itself change its caution level?
6b.description: We applied the same ORPO training to the editor instead of a specialist, using 88 pairs built from saved editor write-ups. The editor's caution level did not move, so training at the editor changed the final answer no more than training at the specialists.
6b.size: 70 runs, after training on 88 example pairs
6b.why: Every training attempt so far had targeted the specialists, and the idea that the editor sets the final level rested on removing parts of the system. The paper's practical advice, to tune the editor, had never been tested. This cell applied the same ORPO method one level up, to the editor. We chose Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: it was already one of Cell 6's editors, it had the highest habitual level, and at 7B it could be trained within the machine's memory. Phi-4 was left for later for the same memory reason. We built training pairs from real editor inputs in saved runs. The preferred answer had caveats added and the rejected one had them removed. All three specialists stayed at their untrained versions.

expectations.text: Training would move the editor's caution level by at least 0.25 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters, with ranges that do not overlap.
expectations.note: The level moved by 0.14, from 1.03 to 0.89, and the ranges overlapped heavily.

expectations.text: The trained editor would be less cautious on the control question than the untrained one, on both scoring methods.
expectations.note: It went from 0.15 to 0.11, the expected direction, but both were already near zero, so we did not claim an effect.

expectations.text: Training the editor would change the final answer more than training any specialist had in Cells 2, 3 and 5.
expectations.note: No. The editor's change was no larger than the specialists' changes, and none stood out from its untrained comparison.

6b.found:
The trained editor's final answers averaged 0.89 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters, against 1.03 for the untrained copy. We had set a change of at least 0.25 with ranges that do not overlap as the bar. The change was a drop of 0.14, and the ranges overlapped heavily. The untrained level was also close to what the same model showed in Cell 6 (1.24), so the level was stable across cells.

On the control question, caution went from 0.15 to 0.11. The untrained editor already scored only 0.15 there, leaving almost nothing to remove, the same situation as Med42 in Cell 3. We did not claim an effect.

Two changes to the plan were written down before training. None of the long editor examples fit the usual training length, so it was raised from 1,792 to 4,096 tokens. Too few pairs passed our filters, mostly because adding caveats made a long write-up too long compared with the original. Rather than loosen the filters, we generated from all 325 saved write-ups instead of 200. The final set had 88 pairs, against 91 planned.
6b.means: Training the last writer on matched examples moved its level no more than training a specialist moved the specialist's. Across three specialists and the editor, with ORPO and CPO and up to 3.2 times more data, weight training never moved the caution in the final answer. What did move it, reliably and 2 to 5 times, was the editor's instruction. We concluded that the editor's habitual level sets the final caution, and that its instructions, not anyone's weights, are the way to change it. The limits: one editor model, 88 pairs instead of 91, only 5 control-question runs near zero, and a longer training length than the specialists had.
6b.later: Cell 11 asked the same question with a different training setup, sampling the editor's own answers and rewarding well-placed caution, and again saw no change. Cell 18 tried a third training goal without improvement, and Cell 16 found that full reinforcement learning (GRPO) would not fit in the machine's memory. STATUS.md still lists as a current claim that preference training does not move this behavior.

522.label: Plan
522.title: Plan: apply the same ORPO training to the editor
522.summary: We would train the editor model, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, on 91 pairs built from real editor inputs, using the specialists' recipe. Then we would run 70 answers with all specialists untrained. We expected its caution level to move, its control-question score to fall, and the effect to exceed any from specialist training.

643.label: Result
643.title: Training the editor did not move its caution level
643.summary: After ORPO on 88 pairs, the editor's final caution was 0.89 against 1.03 untrained, well short of the planned 0.25 change, with overlapping ranges. The control question moved from 0.15 to 0.11, both near zero. We concluded that the editor's instructions, not model weights, are what changes final caution.

6c.title: Do instructions work like a volume knob, and does input add up?
6c.description: We varied how many keep-the-caveats clauses the editor received, from none to all three, and how many specialists were made extra cautious. Caution rose with the clauses for all three editors, but more cautious specialists did not add caution.
6c.size: 96 runs, 72 on the clauses and 24 on the input
6c.why: Cell 6 tested the instruction to keep caveats only as on or off, yet the paper called it a volume knob. A volume knob implies caution rising step by step as more of the instruction is included. The production prompt has three such clauses: keep estimates flagged as estimates, keep precise wording, and keep caveats. We removed them one at a time in a fixed order, with three editors and the 6 scenarios that call for caveats. A second part tested the last alternative to the editor's habitual level: that caution from several specialists partly adds up. With Phi-4 as editor, we made 0 to 3 specialists extra cautious using a prompt that asks for caveats.

expectations.text: Final caution would rise with the number of clauses for every editor, scoring at least 0.8 on a rank measure where 1.0 means caution rose at every step.
expectations.note: All three editors reached the bar (1.0, 0.8 and 0.8), though only gpt-oss-20B rose at every step.

expectations.text: Going from all three clauses to none would change caution by 2 to 6 times, so the instruction shifts the editor's level within limits.
expectations.note: Two editors fell inside the range, at 3.3 and 2.1 times. Phi-4 did not, at 1.3 times, because of one odd result with two clauses.

expectations.text: Final caution would stay flat as more specialists were made extra cautious, with no steady rise (a rank score of 0.4 or less).
expectations.note: It stayed flat or fell slightly, from 1.01 with none to 0.64 with all three, a rank score of minus 0.8.

expectations.text: Changing the order in which specialists answered would change final caution by less than 0.2 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters.
expectations.note: Withdrawn before any runs, because the planning step sets the order and it could not be changed without changing the plan itself.

6c.found:
Caution in the final answer rose as clauses were added, for all three editors. From no clauses to all three, gpt-oss-20B rose from 0.16 to 0.53 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters, rising at every step. Qwen2.5 rose from 0.57 to 1.21, with a small dip at two clauses. Phi-4 rose only from 0.52 to 0.68, with one odd high result of 1.53 at two clauses. Its runs varied as much within that setting as between settings. With 6 runs each and no repeats, we judged it most likely noise and reported it without explaining it away.

Making more specialists extra cautious did not raise the final answer. With 0, 1, 2 or 3 such specialists, it scored 1.01, 1.03, 0.84 and 0.64, with heavily overlapping ranges. Making all three extra cautious gave no more caution than making none.

Before any runs, we corrected the clause count of the full prompt from four to three, and dropped a planned test of specialist order.
6c.means: Together with Cell 6b, the picture for the paper was this. Training moved final caution at neither the specialists nor the editor, and caution from the specialists did not accumulate. The editor's instructions moved it steadily, by 3.3 and 2.1 times for gpt-oss-20B and Qwen2.5. We concluded that the instructions were the practical way to control final caution. The mild fall with more cautious specialists fits Cell 6's finding that very cautious input can lower the output, but we did not claim it.
6c.later: Cell 7c found that no single kind of caveat rose steadily with the clauses, only the combined score. An audit on 1 August reproduced every number but noted that only gpt-oss-20B rose at every step, and the paper's wording was corrected. Cell 13 traced the rise to one clause. PD-13 then found the clauses mostly made the editor type the exact phrases they named, and the claim that instructions work as a volume knob was withdrawn.

561.label: Plan
561.title: Plan: test the instruction in steps, and whether input adds up
561.summary: We would vary the number of keep-the-caveats clauses from 0 to 3 for three editors, in 72 runs. We would also vary the number of extra-cautious specialists from 0 to 3, in 24 runs. Before any runs we corrected the clause count and dropped an order test. This part of the notebook also holds two changes to Cell 6b's plan.

687.label: Result
687.title: Caution rises with the clauses, and specialist input does not add up
687.summary: Final caution rose with the number of clauses for all three editors, most cleanly for gpt-oss-20B, with one odd Phi-4 result. Making more specialists extra cautious gave no more final caution. With Cell 6b, we concluded that the editor's instructions, not training, control final caution.

7.title: Checking how we score caution
7.description: Our plan to strengthen how we score caution was carried out as three separate cells. They added an NLI model as a second scorer (7a), paired AI judges (7b) and a split of scores by kind of caveat (7c).
7.why: Every score so far came from one keyword counter that counted cautious phrases per 1,000 characters. The original plan added three things: an AI judge (gpt-oss-20B), a check of about 50 items against human labels, and scores per claim beside scores per 1,000 characters. The need became pressing when Cell 3's finance result rested on the keyword counter alone.
7.found:
The work ran as three cells. Cell 7a tested an NLI model as a second scorer and re-scored key results with it, counting caveats per 10 sentences. Cell 7b had two AI judges compare pairs of answers. Cell 7c split the existing scores by kind of caveat.

After 7b, the notebook closed Cell 7 with a summary. The lack of a rise in caution after training held on two scoring methods for all three specialists. So did the healthcare specialist's zero on the control question. The legal specialist's drop on that question held on three methods. The finance model's apparent worsening appeared only in the keyword counter and was dropped. The planned check against human labels does not appear in the notebook.
7.means: The early training results were narrowed to what more than one scoring method supported. Two limits were recorded. The NLI model's combined count was spoiled by two kinds of caveat it could not score. The judges' rule of quoting answers word for word was too strict for answers dense with numbers.
7.later: Later work weakened all three methods. Cell 23 found the NLI model could not detect which kinds of caveat a sentence contained. On 11 August the judges' prompt was found to list the same stock phrases that our writing prompts told models to use. From 9 August the keyword counter was no longer accepted as a measuring tool.

7a.title: Does an NLI model agree with our keyword counter?
7a.description: We tested an NLI model as a second way to score caution. It told preferred from rejected training answers apart well, and agreed that training raised no caution. It did not reproduce the finance result and matched the legal one only in part.
7a.size: No new runs, 289 test pairs plus re-scored answers
7a.why: Cell 3's finding that the finance training failed rested entirely on our keyword counter. Before rewriting the paper's second result, we wanted an independent scoring method. We chose a local NLI model (natural-language-inference model) of the DeBERTa-v3 type. It reads each sentence and judges whether it implies a fixed statement, one for each kind of caveat. For estimates, the statement was "The writer labels a number or estimate as an assumption". We first checked it on answer pairs with known labels: the preferred training answers had caveats added and the rejected ones had them removed. Then we fixed its settings and re-scored the key results. Where the two methods agreed, a result would stand. Where they disagreed, it would wait for Cell 7b.

expectations.text: The NLI model would tell preferred training answers from rejected ones with a separation score of at least 0.85, or it would be too weak to settle anything.
expectations.note: It scored 0.929 overall. Two kinds of caveat, hedging and precise wording, could not be scored usefully at their cut-offs.

expectations.text: The NLI model would confirm the legal result: after ORPO, caution on the control question at most half the untouched level.
expectations.note: Failed as planned, because the two broken kinds swamped the combined count. Out-of-date warnings alone fell from 1.06 to 0.35, matching the keyword counter's direction.

expectations.text: The NLI model would confirm the finance result: after ORPO, caution on the control question at least as high as untouched, so the worsening was real.
expectations.note: Failed. No kind of caveat rose, so the apparent worsening appeared only in the keyword counter.

7a.found:
The first check passed. The NLI model separated preferred from rejected answers with a score of 0.929, where 0.5 is a coin toss and 1.0 is perfect. But two of the five kinds of caveat were broken at their chosen cut-offs. At its cut-off the hedging check could not tell answers apart, and the precise-wording check fired on almost every sentence. The out-of-date check was the best calibrated.

As planned, the combined count added all five kinds, so the broken two swamped it, and both tests of past results failed. Other results agreed with the keyword counter: training raised caution on none of the three specialists, and healthcare's zero on the control question matched exactly. We then looked kind by kind, a step we had not planned. On the legal specialist, out-of-date warnings on the control question fell from 1.06 to 0.35, the same direction as the keyword counter. On the finance model nothing rose: out-of-date warnings went from 0.19 to 0.14 and estimate flags from 5.19 to 4.32.

The NLI hedging check fired 4 to 6 times per 10 sentences even on text with caveats stripped out. It seemed to detect conditions in the substance of a claim, not cautious phrasing.
7a.means: Under the rule we set in advance, two results now stood on two methods. They were no rise in caution after training on all three specialists, and healthcare's zero on the control question. The legal drop leaned toward holding up but narrowed to out-of-date warnings, and waited for Cell 7b. The finance worsening was most likely a quirk of the keyword counter. The finance model still showed no drop, so its failure to repeat the legal result stood under both methods.
7a.later: Cell 23 later showed that these settings, tuned to tell training pairs apart, could not detect whether a sentence contained a given kind of caveat. That is how the re-scoring here used them. Their scores ran from below chance to near chance, and too few out-of-date warnings existed to check that kind. The wording "confirmed by two methods" was weakened to "two independent measurements".

303.label: Plan
303.title: Plan: test an NLI model as a second scoring method
303.summary: An NLI model would score each sentence against five fixed statements, one per kind of caveat, and count matches per 10 sentences. We would check it on training pairs with known labels, fix its settings, then re-score the legal, finance and healthcare results. Agreement with the keyword counter would make a result stand.

342.label: Result
342.title: The NLI model passes its check but settles only some results
342.summary: It separated known pairs well (0.929), but two kinds of caveat were broken, spoiling the planned combined count. No rise after training and healthcare's zero now stood on two methods. The legal drop held for out-of-date warnings only, and the finance worsening was not reproduced.

7b.title: Can AI judges settle the disputed legal and finance results?
7b.description: Two local AI judges compared control-question answers from untrained and ORPO specialists, in both orders. Both said the legal ORPO answers hedged less every time. On finance, too few judgments survived to settle anything, so the worsening was dropped.
7b.size: No new runs, about 180 AI judge calls
7b.why: Cell 7a left two results depending on which scoring method we trusted. On the legal specialist, the keyword counter and the NLI out-of-date check showed ORPO cutting caution on the control question, but the planned NLI count did not. On finance, only the keyword counter showed ORPO making things worse. We added a third method: AI judges comparing two answers at a time, never giving absolute scores. For each of the two specialists we paired each of the 5 untrained answers with each of the 5 ORPO answers, 25 pairs. Two judges, gpt-oss-20B and Qwen2.5-7B, saw each pair in both orders without knowing which was which. We counted a matchup only when a judge picked the same winner both times. Every judgment had to quote the answers word for word, or it was thrown out.

expectations.text: On the legal specialist, both judges would say the ORPO answer hedged less in at least 70% of the matchups they decided.
expectations.note: Both judges said so in every decided matchup, 7 of 7 each, and answer length did not explain it.

expectations.text: On the finance specialist, the worsening would count as real only if both judges said the ORPO answer hedged more in at least 70% of decided matchups. The NLI results suggested it would not.
expectations.note: Too few usable judgments: most pairs were thrown out for inexact quotes, leaving 2 decided matchups for one judge and none for the other. The worsening was dropped.

7b.found:
Legal: in every matchup where a judge picked the same winner both times, it said the ORPO answer hedged less. That was 7 of 7 for gpt-oss-20B and 7 of 7 for Qwen2.5. The more-cautious answer was the longer one in only 43% of these, so length did not drive the result. Many matchups were ties, because many ORPO answers contained no hedging at all. The legal drop now held on three methods: the keyword counter (0.96 to 0.15), the NLI out-of-date check (1.06 to 0.35) and the judges (14 of 14).

Finance: 21 to 23 of the 25 pairs per judge were thrown out, because the judges paraphrased their quotes from answers dense with numbers and formatting. Of the rest, gpt-oss-20B decided 2, both saying ORPO hedged more, and Qwen2.5 decided none. In both of those, the answer judged more cautious was also the longer one. The worsening was not confirmed.
7b.means: The legal drop became the paper's one positive result on training, stated narrowly: ORPO reduced unneeded hedging on the legal specialist. For finance, the keyword counter showed a worsening, the NLI model showed none and the judges could not decide, so we dropped the worsening. The finance result became no effect: ORPO did not reduce caution there. This closed Cell 7. We recorded that the word-for-word quote rule was too strict for answers dense with numbers.
7b.later: On 11 August, a registry of the exact wording in our prompts found a problem. The judges' prompt listed the same stock phrases, such as "modeled at" and "this may vary if", that several writing prompts told models to use. The judges were looking for wording the writers had been told to produce. An audit on 5 August had also left the judges' handling of empty replies unchecked, as a low-risk open item.

393.label: Plan
393.title: Plan: two AI judges compare answers in pairs
393.summary: Two local judges would compare 25 pairs of control-question answers per specialist, each pair in both orders, with quotes checked word for word. If both judges found the legal ORPO answer hedging less in at least 70% of decided matchups, the legal drop would stand. The same 70% bar applied to the finance worsening.

424.label: Result
424.title: Judges back the legal drop, and the finance worsening is dropped
424.summary: Both judges said the legal ORPO answers hedged less in every decided matchup, 7 of 7 each, so the legal drop held on three methods. On finance most judgments were thrown out for inexact quotes, the worsening was dropped and finance became no effect. This closed Cell 7.

7c.title: Splitting the results by kind of caveat
7c.description: We split 628 saved runs by kind of caveat and tested each kind on the specialist that produces it. ORPO's lack of effect held for every kind. The editor stripped out-of-date warnings but kept caveats that carry content, and one kind was never detected.
7c.size: No new runs, re-scored 628 saved runs
7c.why: Our combined score adds up five kinds of caveat, but the specialists do not produce them equally. Scoring all five on one specialist, as our main tables did, let out-of-date warnings dominate and understated kinds that are common elsewhere. So we split the existing results by kind and tested each kind on the specialist that produces it most. No new answers were generated.
7c.found:
Each kind had a home. Before training, out-of-date warnings appeared on all three specialists. Estimate flags came only from finance, hedging from healthcare and finance, and rules-differ-by-place warnings weakly from legal. Precise-wording caveats were below detection everywhere, at 0.00 to 0.02 per 1,000 characters.

Tested on its home specialist, ORPO changed no kind. Estimate flags on finance went from 0.40 to 0.34, hedging on healthcare from 0.33 to 0.26, and place warnings on legal from 0.14 to 0.18, all with overlapping ranges. Training the editor in Cell 6b changed none of the four detectable kinds either. Prompting and SFT did change the legal specialist. Prompting raised its out-of-date warnings from 0.68 to 1.46 and SFT to 1.21. SFT also added estimate flags and hedging, which it had rarely or never produced, and cut its place warnings from 0.14 to 0.02.

The editor did not strip all kinds equally. With untrained specialists, and measured against the home specialist, the final answer kept 69% of out-of-date warnings and 76% of hedging. Estimate flags and place warnings came out at 105% and 125%. Across the three editors, no single kind rose steadily with the number of keep-the-caveats clauses. Only the combined score did. Making more specialists extra cautious raised no kind in the final answer.
7c.means: Two claims got stronger. ORPO's lack of effect was not an artifact of out-of-date warnings, and prompting and SFT added several kinds of caveat. One claim was narrowed: the step-by-step rise with the clauses holds for the combined score, not for each kind. One finding was new, an observation rather than a planned test. The editor keeps caveats that carry content, like an estimated figure or a rule that differs by place. It strips out-of-date warnings, which it can cut without losing content. The paper would now speak of four detectable kinds, with the combined score dominated by out-of-date warnings.
7c.later: Cell 13 found the combined score is dominated by out-of-date warnings only for the Qwen2.5 and Phi-4 editors, not for gpt-oss-20B, which almost never gives them. Cell 23 then found the keyword counter caught about 92% of estimate flags, but only 25 to 30% of hedging and place warnings and none of 3 out-of-date warnings. The kind-by-kind figures here are therefore provisional.

733.label: Result
733.title: Scores split by kind of caveat: what changes and what holds
733.summary: Re-scoring 628 saved runs by kind showed ORPO changed no kind on the specialist that produces it, while prompting and SFT raised several. The editor kept content-carrying caveats but stripped part of the out-of-date warnings. Precise-wording caveats were never detected, leaving four usable kinds.

setup.title: The original plan: nine expectations and ten cells
setup.description: Before any cell ran, we wrote down nine expectations and ten planned cells. They would test whether our first result held across specialists, base models, training methods and editors, at no cost on one machine.
setup.why: Our first result came from one run per scenario on one specialist, the legal model Saul. It suggested that ORPO preference training made caution better targeted and helped it survive the editor. On 11 July we planned a campaign to turn this into a claim that held across several specialists and base models, with parts removed to see what changed. Everything had to run locally with no spending on paid AI services, and we wrote down the expectations before any cell ran.
setup.found:
The nine expectations were these. P1: preference training beats training on good examples alone. P2: ORPO repeats the legal result on the finance specialist. P3: the healthcare specialist, already preference-trained by its makers, gains less than the finance one. P4: the effect is smaller on other, more heavily aligned base models. P5: CPO repeats ORPO's result. P6: caveats survive with all three local editors, and prompted caution weakens without the keep-the-caveats instruction. P7: without any training by us, OpenBioLLM-8B, which its makers trained with DPO, scores high on caution and BioMistral-7B, which had only pretraining, scores low. P8: caveats from training sit in the same sentence as specific facts, unlike prompted ones, and such caveats survive the editor better. P9: training on three kinds of caveat does not raise the other two.

The ten cells tested P1 to P8, plus five runs per setup, better scoring and an outside benchmark. P9 had no cell. Two limits were accepted. A documented bug ruled out DPO itself, so claims would cover only ORPO and CPO, preference methods that need no reference model. There would be no cell with a frontier model, one of the most capable large models, as the editor. A recovery note said an earlier cleanup had deleted intermediate training files, and that Cell 1 would re-download and convert Saul, taking about 20 minutes.
setup.means: The plan changed as results came in. Cells 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 10 were carried out, and Cell 7 was carried out as Cells 7a, 7b and 7c. Cells 4 and 9 were never run. P7's version with the models as specialists was retired before any data. The comparison moved to Cell 8b, with the models as editors, and the number 8 went to an architecture comparison. P9 does not appear again. New cells, starting with 6b and 6c, were added as results raised new questions.
setup.later: A note of 28 July clarified that the plan's P8 is unrelated to Cell 8's expectations P8.1 to P8.3, which share the number only by coincidence. P8 itself did not hold up when Cell 10 tested it.

entry-7.label: Plan
entry-7.title: Nine expectations written down before any cell ran
entry-7.summary: A table of nine expectations, P1 to P9, each with the result that would prove it wrong. They covered preference training against training on examples, other specialists, other base models and a second training method. They also covered the editors, untrained medical models, caveats tied to facts, and whether training on some kinds of caveat lifts others.

entry-21.label: Plan
entry-21.title: Ten planned cells and what each would test
entry-21.summary: A numbered list of ten cells. SFT against ORPO came first, then five runs per setup, finance and healthcare specialists, other base models and CPO. Then came three editors with and without the keep-the-caveats instruction, better scoring, two more medical specialists, an outside benchmark, and a check of whether caveats sit next to specific facts.

entry-41.label: Note
entry-41.title: Limits accepted to keep the cost at zero
entry-41.summary: Everything would run locally with no spending. A documented bug in the DPO training software meant claims would cover only ORPO and CPO, two preference methods that need no reference model. No frontier model would serve as the editor, so findings about the editor would cover local models only.

entry-46.label: Note
entry-46.title: Recovering deleted training files
entry-46.summary: An earlier cleanup had deleted intermediate training files, but every recipe was saved. Cell 1 would re-download the legal model, Saul, and convert it again, which takes about 20 minutes.

writing-notes.title: Early notes on framing the paper, and a glossary
writing-notes.description: On the day Cell 1 finished, we sketched how the paper should be built and what it should claim. Soon after, we wrote a glossary of terms every write-up had to define, from specialist and editor to the five kinds of caveat.
writing-notes.why: Cell 1 seemed to confirm our main idea, so we wrote down how the paper should present it. Soon after, we added a glossary so that the paper, the README and the results page would all define the same working terms in the same way.
writing-notes.found:
The framing notes treated the council as both the test bed and a finding in its own right. The paper would open with the setup. It had a planning step, three specialists and an editor that lists disagreements before writing. It used 7 scenarios and two kinds of score, one for content and one for caution. Result 1 would be that the council's structure raises caution, 3 to 9 times on one measure, whatever the model. Result 2 would compare three ways of adding caution to a specialist: prompting, SFT and ORPO. Result 3 would be that only preference-trained caution survives the editor. Earlier negative results on what specialists add in content would serve as background. The notes warned against framing the paper as specialists against frontier models, a crowded topic that our own earlier data had already undercut.

The glossary defined a specialist, the editor (then Phi-4 14B) and the loss of caution between them. It defined caution as what a model chooses to say, separate from what it knows. It listed the five kinds of caveat, with hedging meaning a stated condition under which a claim could change, not refusal or vagueness. It separated caution that appears only when called for from caution that appears regardless. It scored caution per 1,000 characters and with a combined score, CDS = density × √breadth. Here density is caveats per 1,000 characters and breadth is how many kinds of caveat appear.
writing-notes.means: These notes set out the story the project first tried to tell. Preference training at the specialist decides when a model is cautious, and only that caution survives the editor. The glossary fixed the working terms used in the cells that followed.
writing-notes.later: The framing soon changed. Cell 2 found ORPO's advantage in the final answer was noise and revised the one-sentence summary. Cell 8 found the council's rise in caution came from its instruction, not its multi-agent structure, and on 1 August the paper was retitled around a new account. Cell 7c cut the five kinds of caveat to four detectable ones.

entry-73.label: Note
entry-73.title: How the paper should be structured and framed
entry-73.summary: Written the day Cell 1 finished, it treated the council as both test bed and finding. It planned three results: the structure raises caution, three ways of adding caution compared, and only preference-trained caution survives the editor. It warned against framing the paper as specialists against frontier models.

entry-126.label: Note
entry-126.title: Glossary of working terms for every write-up
entry-126.summary: Definitions that the paper, README and results page all had to use. They covered the specialist, the editor, the loss of caution between them, and caution as what a model chooses to say. They also listed the five kinds of caveat, separated targeted from habitual caution, and defined alignment as the training that follows pretraining.

dose.title: Does training on more example pairs change anything?
dose.description: We retrained the legal specialist with ORPO on 292 pairs, 3.2 times the original 91. Its caution did not change at all, and its drop in caution on the control question became smaller, not larger.
dose.why: Cell 2 showed that ORPO with 91 training pairs added almost no caution to the legal specialist. Its one distinctive effect was less caution on the control question. That made the amount of training data the first open question: would more pairs build up caution gradually? We trained a second ORPO version on 292 pairs, 3.2 times as many, matched for the number of passes through the data. We ran it 5 times on each of the 7 scenarios.
dose.found:
More data changed nothing at the specialist. Caution was 0.84 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters with 292 pairs, 0.85 with 91 pairs and 0.84 for the untouched copy. This held even though the new version had learned the preference far better. On pairs held back from training, it ranked the preferred answer above the rejected one 94% of the time, against about 48% for the first version.

The drop on the control question weakened. The first version had scored 0.15 there, against 0.96 for the untouched copy. The new version scored 0.49, still below the untouched copy but a smaller effect. A tentative reading was that more varied pairs slightly widened where the model hedges. On the combined caution score for the final answer, the new version scored 0.689, against 0.655 for the first and 0.849 for the untouched copy.
dose.means: The amount of preference data did not set how much caution the specialist showed. The limit on caution in the final answer was the editor's habitual level, found in Cell 6. What preference training adds is less unneeded hedging, and even that did not grow with more data and may have faded. For the paper, the question of data amount was settled. Three times more data did not raise the specialist's caution, and ORPO's value lies in targeting, not in adding caution.
dose.later: Cells 6b, 11 and 18 found that training the editor did not change its behavior either. STATUS.md lists as a current claim that preference training does not move this behavior, citing the rise from 48% to 94% with behavior unchanged. The keyword-counter scores here are treated as provisional.

entry-209.label: Result
entry-209.title: Three times more training data leaves caution unchanged
entry-209.summary: ORPO on 292 pairs learned the preference far better than on 91 pairs. Yet caution stayed at 0.84 cautious phrases per 1,000 characters, no different from 91 pairs (0.85) or the untouched copy (0.84). Its drop on the control question weakened, from 0.15 to 0.49. ORPO's value lies in targeting, not in adding caution.
